topic: Diagnosing circular reasoning and unsupported proof statements

problems.desc: part (a): the faulty line is step 3, whose reason is the statement itself -- the proof offers the congruence of the two angles as the reason for that same congruence, so nothing new is ever established. A correct response points at step 3 and says the reason repeats the claim.

part (b): a valid replacement reason is the vertical angles theorem, since the two angles are the opposite pair formed by the two intersecting lines named in the given. Any reason that traces back to the given, and not to the conclusion, earns full credit.

part (a): the error is in the second line, where 6 was added to the left side only. The addition property of equality requires the same quantity on both sides, so the right side should have become 2x + 16.

traps.desc: added 6 to the left side only, leaving the right side as 2x + 10

problems.desc: part (a): step 2 is unsupported. Nothing in the given says the ray divides the angle into two congruent parts, and a drawing that looks even is not evidence -- the reason column cites the figure rather than a given, a definition or a theorem.

part (b): the proof becomes valid if the given list is extended to say that the ray bisects the angle, or if the figure carries matching congruence marks on the two smaller angles; the reason on step 2 would then be the definition of an angle bisector.

part (a): the setup is right but the third line is wrong -- 3 was subtracted from both sides when it should have been added, so the right-hand constant became 6 instead of 12. The definition of midpoint and the equation that follows from it are both correct.

traps.desc: subtracted 3 from both sides instead of adding it, so 3x = 6

problems.desc: part (a): the two claims support each other and nothing else supports either, so the argument is circular. A correct response says that the congruence of the corresponding angles is used to prove the lines parallel and is then itself justified by the lines being parallel.

part (b): a repaired argument starts from something independently known. Either the angle measures are given or measured, so the corresponding angles are congruent and the converse of the corresponding angles postulate gives the parallel lines; or the lines are given parallel and the corresponding angles postulate gives the congruence. One direction only, with a starting point outside the pair of claims.

part (a): step 2 is unsupported and its reason is wrong. The two angles form a linear pair, not a vertical pair, so they are supplementary rather than congruent; the correct reason is the linear pair postulate and the correct statement is that the two measures add to 180.

traps.desc: treated the linear pair as vertical angles and set the two measures equal
